answer.decision: Add jittered expirations, request coalescing, and stale-while-revalidate.
answer.action: Today, enable single-flight for same-key cache misses and allow one request to refresh an entry while concurrent requests receive stale data. Cap stale serving at both 90 seconds and five minutes of total data age. Follow up by replacing deterministic TTLs with bounded randomized jitter, configuring the fresh TTL and stale window so their combined worst case never exceeds five minutes, and monitoring cache hit rate, origin requests by key, coalesced requests, stale serves, refresh latency and failures, and maximum served-data age.
reasons: Repeated work is the primary failure mode: 91 percent of the origin CPU spike came from duplicate queries for only 120 keys.
The existing single-flight capability can immediately suppress concurrent same-key origin queries without replacing the cache product.
Jitter reduces synchronized expirations, while stale-while-revalidate prevents refreshes from producing bursts of misses.
A 90-second stale window is acceptable when enforced within the five-minute total-age requirement.
Database scaling improved query latency but did not prevent saturation, and a global TTL increase could violate the freshness constraint.
assumptions: The existing single-flight primitive can be enabled today without changing cache products.
Cached records include, or can be given, a trustworthy origin timestamp so total data age can be enforced.
The cache can retain entries beyond their fresh TTL for the bounded stale-while-revalidate window.
risks: Refresh failures could breach the freshness requirement unless stale responses are rejected once total data age reaches five minutes.
Single-flight may leave callers waiting behind a slow refresh; bounded waits, timeouts, and controlled failure behavior are required.
A poorly bounded jitter distribution could still cluster expirations or make the fresh TTL plus stale window exceed five minutes.
Evictions, cold starts, or cache outages can bypass these protections and may require origin load shedding or rate limiting.

citations.claim: Ninety-one percent of the origin CPU spike came from repeated queries for the same 120 keys.
The cache client library already provides a disabled single-flight primitive.
The endpoint must keep data age within five minutes.
Database scale-up reduced query latency but did not prevent saturation under repeated duplicate requests.
Stale values may be served for up to 90 seconds during refresh if the five-minute freshness bound is preserved.
